Friends both, go join you with some further aid:
Hamlet in madness hath Polonius slain,
And from his mother’s closet hath he dragg’d him:
Go seek him out; speak fair, and bring the body
Into the chapel. I pray you, haste in this. Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.
Come, Gertrude, we’ll call up our wisest friends;
And let them know, both what we mean to do,
And what’s untimely done. So haply slander—
Whose whisper o’er the world’s diameter,
As level as the canon to his blank,
Transports his poison’d shot, may miss our name,
And hit the woundless air. O, come away!
My soul is full of discord and dismay. Exeunt.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Mad as the sea and wind, when both contend / Which is the mightier” slowly and put it in my own words: Gertrude tells Claudius that Hamlet is as mad as the sea and wind fighting over which is stronger. Next, craft. I notice the storm simile, which makes his madness a natural force. The strongest word is “mightier”: it shows a struggle with no winner, which fits Hamlet's inner battle. Then, effect. How does Gertrude describe Hamlet's state to Claudius? My answer: Gertrude protects Hamlet by insisting he is mad, not dangerous; the image also shows the turmoil she has seen, and Claudius decides to send him to England.
